sections.title: The Hook: Dynamics in Motion
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a rate of change using a visual of a cheetah chasing prey. Emphasize that we often know how fast something is changing (velocity/acceleration) but need to find the position function over time.
sections.example: A cheetah's velocity is proportional to its distance from the prey; how do we describe its position at any time t?

sections.title: Defining the ODE: The Mathematical Bridge
sections.content: Define an ODE as an equation involving a function and its derivatives. Use a graphical split-screen: the left side shows a slope field (arrows representing local derivatives), and the right side shows a smooth curve (the solution) threading through the field.
sections.example: dy/dt = ky (The growth of a bacterial colony where the rate of growth is proportional to the current population size).

sections.title: The Core Mechanics: Solving via Integration
sections.content: Explain that solving an ODE is essentially 'reversing' the derivative. Visually demonstrate the process by 'integrating' the slope field arrows to reconstruct the function path.
sections.example: Given dy/dt = 2t, we integrate both sides to find y(t) = t² + C, where 'C' represents the family of all possible starting positions.

sections.title: Initial Conditions: Pinning Down the Solution
sections.content: Explain the role of the constant 'C'. Use a visual 'slider' that moves the solution curve up and down; show that a single point (Initial Condition) is required to select the specific curve from the family of solutions.
sections.example: If the bacterial colony starts with 10 cells at t=0, C=10, giving us the unique solution y(t) = 10e^(kt).

sections.title: Real-World Synthesis & Wrap-up
sections.content: Summarize that ODEs are the language of change. Revisit the cheetah example: by knowing the physics (derivative), we solve the equation (integral) to predict exactly where the cheetah will be at any time.
sections.example: Applying ODEs to a smartphone battery drain: dV/dt = -k(V) helps us predict exactly when the device will turn off.
